title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. The remainin
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack.Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they meanThe company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

schema.headline: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack

title: King to address slavery during Commonwealth speech in Antigua on final leg of Caribbean tour
description: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final le
body: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.The King will make his speech at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said."You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK Government's position".The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the "suffering of the past".In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed. Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace."His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", external, and that Britain "must face up to the past".His pledge to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by King Charles, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change."Institutions are under strain across the globe," said a Palace spokesperson. "The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua, and they will attend a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island.

schema.headline: King to address slavery during Commonwealth speech in Antigua on final leg of Caribbean tour

title: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
description: Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.Last weekend, the DE civic ac
body: Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina. During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students. A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used."From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything." Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs. A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force. Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment. An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number."It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC."The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power. The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other. Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement. "There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC. "In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

schema.headline: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán

title: Second night of drone disruption at Jersey Airport
description: The Chief Minister of Jersey, Senator Lyndon Farnham, said operating a drone close to an airport was "not a prank or a harmless hobby"."To those respo
body: The Chief Minister of Jersey, Senator Lyndon Farnham, said operating a drone close to an airport was "not a prank or a harmless hobby"."To those responsible, the message is clear: if you are identified, you should expect to face the full consequences of the law," he added.Pacific Basirwe was waiting for his wife and young son to fly in from London Heathrow when he heard the news.He said: "It's annoying, this should be regulated, and the people doing those things should be prosecuted."It's been two days in a row now… If there is no further action, they will keep doing it, which is not good."

title: Stranded in the Cook Islands: Why I can't get home to Sri Lanka
description: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly homeImage source, SuppliedByAyeshea PereraAsia Digital Editor a
body: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly homeImage source, SuppliedByAyeshea PereraAsia Digital Editor and Dinuk HewawitharanaBBC SinhalaWhen Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving."My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears."I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.It turned out to be a disastrous decision.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Cook Islands is known for its beaches and volcanic peaks - but Ruchira Ranasingha is an involuntary guestShe was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do"."She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected."I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.Image source, SuppliedOn a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income."My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says."I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried."Her mental state is not good," her tells BBC Sinhala."One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."Additional reporting by Kethaki Masilamani and Julianna KhanIf you've been affected by issues involving suicide or feelings of despair, details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line. Help and support outside the UK can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.

schema.headline: Stranded in the Cook Islands: Why I can't get home to Sri Lanka

title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
description: The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty clean
body: The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins."We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal."It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area."I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".

schema.headline: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests

title: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
description: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted."When I visited the place for a viewing there was a
body: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted."When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says."Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in."I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties."[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US. But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

schema.headline: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters

title: Manchester United: Are Old Trafford club really heading for a relegation scrap?
description: You would have to be touching 60 to have any recollection of the last time United were relegated.Legend has it that old boy Denis Law sent them down w
body: You would have to be touching 60 to have any recollection of the last time United were relegated.Legend has it that old boy Denis Law sent them down with an impudent back heel he didn't celebrate when he was at Manchester City. The reality is United were already doomed under then-boss Tommy Docherty.United have not been in the relegation zone after nine games or more since November 1986, when they collected a single point in Sir Alex Ferguson's first two games in charge following Ron Atkinson's dismissal.Their lowest position after at least nine games of a season since then was 17th in 1989-90. They are back there again right now, mainly thanks to the failings of others in results elsewhere on Saturday.It is now nine games in all competitions since Carrick's side won, their worst run since 1988-89. Their single Premier League win of the season was when they came from behind to beat Ipswich at home in August.Of course, United's supporters have very recent experience of seeing their team in the lower reaches of the table. They were 16th under Ruben Amorim after 37 games of the 2024-25 season. The caveat is they were 14 points clear of third-bottom Leicester and at no point in that tortuous campaign were they in danger of relegation.One club that has been at real risk in recent years is Tottenham, who were third bottom and two points behind West Ham with four games of last season remaining.So, it could happen, even if it remains unlikely a club that should post revenues in excess of £700m for the current campaign will finish in the bottom three."You can look at it like that, or you can look at how far you can move up the league quite quickly if you win football matches," was Carrick's response when asked if his players are equipped for the "mentality shift" required to deal with the present situation. "That's the way it's got to be approached."Yet, as Carrick said, in order to save themselves, United need to win matches.Their next game is against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on 8 November. Among the seven matches they have after that are trips to Liverpool, Newcastle and Arsenal.As yet, there is no word about Carrick's future, although before Saturday's loss, the expectation was he would be in charge for Tuesday's Champions League encounter with Roma.But these are unchartered waters and no-one can be absolutely sure what happens next. It is clear that many players need to improve their performance levels.United will be without one of those players, Lisandro Martinez, who will miss the Villa game due to suspension after his red card at Chelsea, which was branded "inexplicable" by former World Cup final official Darren Cann on BBC Sport.Martinez's longer-term future with the club is uncertain, but clearly he could not leave until January at the earliest.His contract expires in the summer, and the Argentine's patchy injury record had already raised questions over whether it was worth triggering the clause that would commit United to another season.After just nine games, it is a bit early to dig into the actual consequences of relegation for United, but the numbers might offer pause for thought.In May, respected football finance blogger Paul Quinn, known as The Esk, calculated that Tottenham's "absolute revenue loss", external would be between £197m-£235m if they did go down.As one of the league's highest recipients of TV income, United would not remotely be covered by the parachute payments available to relegated clubs.It seems unlikely that many, if any, of their squad would have relegation clauses, and while United have huge commercial income, it is not known to what extent that would be affected by clauses triggered by relegation.United also have £1.15bn worth of debt, made up of bonds that were renegotiated in June at a higher interest rate, a revolving credit facility and outstanding transfer fee payments.The club are also about to launch a fan consultation before coming up with final plans for a new stadium, which are due to be submitted either in late 2027 or early 2028.United fans once again chanted their opposition to a new stadium at Stamford Bridge during the Chelsea defeat.It is a complicated picture, and even though it seems highly unlikely that the doomsday scenario will become reality, the mere fact that United are in the position they are underlines just how poor their form has been.

schema.headline: Manchester United: Are Old Trafford club really heading for a relegation scrap?

title: Who are the real winners of The Celebrity Traitors? Miranda Hart, King Kenny and Maya Jama stand out
description: Image source, BBC/Studio LambertByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors finalIn som
body: Image source, BBC/Studio LambertByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors finalIn some ways, all the players on the Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart, King Kenny, Maya Jama and Joanne McNally, who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.Miranda HartAfter a spell of ill-health, the show has done wonders for bringing Miranda Hart back into the public eye.There was that incredible “Little Mix Big Mix” viral dance moment, but Hart also displayed a level of vulnerability which stood out in a show where the stars don't really talk about their personal lives.When her friend Joe Lycett was banished, her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment."Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.When she was murdered, she also demonstrated genuine emotion in her response. "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary," she said.For culture journalist Natalie Jamieson, Hart's openness and relatability made her the "standout" star from this year's series.And it could also lead to us seeing more of Hart on the small screen. According to The Sun, external, the BBC is looking to bring back her self-titled sitcom after her stint on Celebrity Traitors led to fresh interest in the show.Image source, BBC/Studio LambertImage caption, James AcasterThe BBC declined to comment on the possible return of Hart’s show.But she’s not the only one who won hearts by showing real warmth.The same could be said for Romesh Ranganathan - who, in a departure from his usual cynical, deadpan stand-up persona, seemed really to care about his fellow cast members. Jerry Hall also won viewers over with her charming eccentricity.And then there’s James Acaster, who showed genuine vulnerability as he struggled to come to terms with being a traitor.Social media users seemed split after his bombshell confession to being a traitor, with some totally exasperated and others saying they respected him for going out on his own terms. Either way, he's definitely got the nation talking.King KennyWhen it comes to celebrities who are most likely to see the biggest career boost, most experts say Kenny is King.Going into the castle, the 29-year-old was best known to younger fans as a member of the popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad.But Kenny will have been "the least familiar name to a mainstream audience," says showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.That all changed as he was recruited as a traitor, bringing much-needed energy to the turret - and he made it all the way through to Friday night’s tense final.Having shown he can hold his own alongside established broadcasters, actors and comedians, big things could now be in store for Kenny."He 100% has just been minted as a mainstream star now," said Marina Hyde, on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.“The next steps could be panel shows, presenting roles, reality competitions or entertainment formats,” adds TV reporter Siobhan Synnot.Maya JamaFellow traitor Maya Jama also sailed all the way to the final with her cool-as-a-cucumber persona making her a traitor to be reckoned with.Despite being banished in dramatic fashion, she could now be in line to receive £1m per deal, according to a report in The Times earlier this week, external.What Celebrity Traitors has done for Jama is allow her to reveal more of her personality than on Love Island, says Onafuye.But TV reporter Synnot thinks between the two, Kenny has more to gain because he has introduced himself to millions of new viewers - whereas Jama was already one of Britain's best-known TV presenters before Celebrity Traitors."Maya's gain is subtler: she can emerge looking less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star," she says.Joanne McNallyOf all the comedians in the castle, Joanne McNally was initially the least well known, says Caroline Frost, TV editor at Radio Times.But she flourished on the show, lasting right up to Thursday's semi-final."And she's taken her own path, ignoring the herd and making her own voting decisions, sometimes chaotically, but always with charm, wit and good humour,” says Frost.The Irish comedian's podcast was already popular before the show.But after her stint as the joker of the pack, bigger things could now lie in store for her.Just a few days ago, it was announced, external that her stand-up tour has been extended into 2027, "due to phenomenal demand".And her agents will be "fielding calls" for her to bring her star power to other shows, adds Frost.As it happened: Relive the Celebrity Traitors finalCulture journalist Jamieson says some of the other female contestants - such as Sharon Rooney, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Myha'la - also stood out for showing their wit and wisdom, which could serve them well in the outside world.Things got a bit awkward in one of the episodes, when Sharon disagreed with some of the cast on a challenge, with some social media users saying she was acting in a "childish" way.But others argued it was a classic case of women being drowned out by men."There's been a subtlety in the smartness of women on display here, alongside the frustration of not always being listened to in the game," says Jamieson.Sebastian 'Bash' CroftIn the end, it was faithful duo Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian ‘Bash’ Croft who emerged victorious.Comedian Ranganathan was already a huge star, but the show has introduced Croft, 24, to a much wider audience.He’s had previous acting roles in Game of Thrones and Heartstopper, but Traitors allowed him to show his own personality, "which as we've seen has endeared him both to other players and the huge watching audience", says Frost.He is also building his career as a pop star, and he's had a strong presence on social media during the series, posting videos of his tracks.His debut EP comes out later in November, perfect timing to capitalise on his Traitors win.And what's in store for the others...What's clear is that the true victors aren't necessarily the ones who get their hands on the prize pot.Arguably, what matters most is the amount of screen time you get - and what you do with it.On that note, spare a thought for those who left the show early, such as Amol Rajan, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry.But all made an impact in their own way and, as Synnot points out, they get "a nice anecdote" for future interviews.And what of James Blunt, who stole hearts with his military approach to the challenges and eccentric Top Gun-style outfits - and who came so close to winning the whole show?Maybe he's the mystery man in contention for the new James B(ond) - although his hapless theories could mean he'll be in line to be the new Johnny English instead.

schema.headline: Who are the real winners of The Celebrity Traitors? Miranda Hart, King Kenny and Maya Jama stand out

title: The Stroud woman whose short story inspired Hollywood film Wicker
description: Author's camping trip inspired Hollywood film WickerImage source, Black BearImage caption, The film Wicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October, w
body: Author's camping trip inspired Hollywood film WickerImage source, Black BearImage caption, The film Wicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October, was based on Ursula Wills' short storyBySacha BigwoodReporting fromGloucestershireAn author who was inspired to write a short story after seeing wicker sculptures on a camping trip has said she never imagined it would become a raunchy A-list feature film.Ursula Wills from Stroud, in Gloucestershire, had just returned from a holiday in Cornwall in 2006 when she wrote The Wicker Husband, which follows an ostracised fisherwoman who pays a basket-maker to weave her a husband.The story was picked up by writers who "livened it up" for the big screen to become Wicker, starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Peter Dinklage.Wills called it a "unique and amazing" film that she thinks "audiences are going to go crazy for".The author, who completed a Master of Arts degree at Bath Spa University in 2004, and spent 19 years living in Bristol, drew inspiration for the 14-page story on a camping trip."I'd visited this place called Melinsey Mill, which is an old watermill, where a basket maker had created an art trail around the pond, with big wicker sculptures like a stag, a giant spider, and a wicker man fishing, and I thought what would anyone want a wicker man for?" she said."I had the idea for the story straight away."Figure caption, Author Ursula Wills speaks to BBC Local Radio. Picture: Black BearWills posted The Wicker Husband on a short story website called East of the Web. After racking up interest from readers, she was contacted by actor Rhys Jennings who, alongside Olivier Award–winning composer Darren Clark, created a musical.In March 2020, it opened at Watermill Theatre in Newbury, but after only four nights the theatre had to close because of the Covid-19 pandemic.Image source, Mark Dawson PhotographyImage caption, Ursula Wills is the author of the short story, 'The Wicker Husband' which has been transformed into a feature filmA year later, she was approached by producer Justin Lothrop who asked her for film rights."I had a meeting with writers and directors, but after Olivia Colman came onboard in 2023 things rolled out really fast," Wills said."By the end of 2024 I was out in Budapest where the film was being shot."When I read the script, I thought it was going to be good, and when I saw it being shot in Hungary I knew it - the end result is something unique and amazing. "I think audiences are going to go crazy for it."Image source, Tor Books UKImage caption, Ursula Wills' story has been translated into German and ItalianWicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October and has been described as a raunchy fantasy rom-com, has garnered lots of attention online and spawned countless viral posts.Although Wills has said the finished film remains faithful to her original short story, the intimate relationship between the fisherwoman and her wicker husband has been embellished to "liven it up".Joint writer-directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson said they "loved it immediately". "It was very sort of sparsely written, but just had these beautiful little clues throughout that suggested to us what the tone of the film could become," they explained."We realised this was more than a period fable. We immediately saw a satirical comedy about sex and marriage, a unique visual spectacle, and a strange love story that would ground it all."Image source, Black BearImage caption, Peter Dinklage's character was inspired by the art trail at Melinsey MillThe UK premiere for the film was held earlier this month at the British Film Institute in London. For Wills it was not all glamourous."I had to scuttle away from the afterparty at 21:45 to get the train back to Swindon and then I had to get a rail replacement bus to Stroud," she said.Wills now has a literary agent, and has a new collection of 13 short stories coming out across the world in April.However, she explained the journey of The Wicker Husband was not over yet."I wouldn't have predicted that it was going to be a full film with an A-list cast, but I did think that it would find a home somewhere," she said."It's got legs and it's not finished walking yet".Get in touchYour Voice

title: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
description: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentiall
body: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise. In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.  Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour. In a BBC interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election. It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers. "There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said. "I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages.""I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."

schema.headline: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers

title: Mexico City Grand Prix qualifying result: Lewis Hamilton takes pole position
description: Lewis Hamilton has claimed his first pole position for Ferrari and his first for more than three years at the Mexico City Grand Prix.The seven-time F1
body: Lewis Hamilton has claimed his first pole position for Ferrari and his first for more than three years at the Mexico City Grand Prix.The seven-time F1 champion beat Mercedes' George Russell by 0.009 seconds as the two drivers who can potentially stop Kimi Antonelli clinching the world title on Sunday locked out the front row.Antonelli qualified fifth behind Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Red Bull's Max Verstappen, but will start fourth because of a one-place penalty for the Dutchman.The only way Antonelli can be prevented from winning the title is if Russell wins and the Italian finishes lower than ninth, or if Hamilton wins and Antonelli is out of the points.Hamilton's pole is his first since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, three years and three months ago, and the 105th of his career.He is the oldest driver to secure a pole since Mario Andretti for Ferrari at the 1982 Italian Grand Prix.He and Russell both went out early for their first runs and had to watch as their rivals sought and failed to beat them.Leclerc went first, falling short of Hamilton by 0.119secs. Antonelli was never on target but Verstappen was fastest of all after two sectors and on course to take pole.But the Dutchman locked up into the hairpin in the stadium section and ruined his lap."Oh man, I'm lost for words," said Hamilton. "It's been a really challenging weekend - we had the engine issue yesterday, which meant we were on the back foot and didn't do a long run."We've done a really good job on the setup and to have pole here, wow, it feels special. It's my first pole for Ferrari, and 105th, I like that number."To have your first Ferrari pole, it takes me back to watching Michael [Schumacher] get all those poles when he was at Ferrari and all those wins."Hamilton had been only fourth on the first runs, more than 0.4secs off Leclerc's pace-setting time. But on his final run, he said: "I don't think I lost any time anywhere. It was a super-good lap."Russell, who said he was happy to have ended a run of difficult form but could not explain why, took a unilateral decision not to do a preparation lap after his out lap on his final run.He said he had a "gut feeling" that it was the best approach, but the team had insisted on a prep lap and had fuelled the car for the extra mileage."[The time loss for the extra fuel weight is] such a small number," said Russell, "but it's bigger than the gap to pole. Nevertheless, I'm just happy to be up here."Verstappen said traffic with another car is what led to his loss of time."Already going into (Turn) 12 I had a car very close to me and I already lost time there with the dirty air," he said."And then going into the hairpin, instead of going on the left, I had one car on my right where you normally want to open up the corner. So its a bit of an awkward angle you have to go into the hairpin."Plus you lose your reference on the right-hand side where you are constantly looking. It's a difficult corner to get right, that killed my lap. The most promising thing is how we turned it around as in practice I was not that happy and we turned it around, I was in the fight for pole."McLaren's Lando Norris had looked in contention for pole, fastest in the second session and on the first runs in the final session, when he was third fastest behind Leclerc and Verstappen.But he failed to improve on his final lap and had to be satisfied fight sixth."Just not quick enough that's all," said Norris. "The lap was incredible in Q2 to put me P1. That was very unrealistic in terms of achieving that again in Q3."I am pretty happy with P6, can't ask a lot more and pretty happy with the job I did with the car I have."Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, Racing Bulls pair Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad and Alpine's Pierre Gasly completed the top 10.Lawson was later disqualified from qualifying for an Infringement of the technical regulations regarding the usage of the electrical deployment of the power unit and will start from the back. Fernando Alonso looked to be in contention for his best qualifying of the year for Aston Martin when he went fastest on his first lap of the session ahead of a number of cars that for most of the season have been ahead of him.But his engine suffered a water leak in the energy recovery system as he started his second attempt, when he was still lying third, and he was ordered to stop the car on track.Alonso's frustration after a year of poor performance and reliability from the Honda engine was clear in an interview with the official television channel afterwards, when he said a total of nine words in answer to four questions.In those words, he confirmed it had been an engine problem, said "it was" a good opportunity and it was "correct" that the car has been looking good all weekend - but that he could not do anything in the race "from the back".

title: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
description: Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.Firms
body: Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend."This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers."There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."And neoclouds have benefitted.But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable. "Some will make it through, but not many," he added.For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity."There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

schema.headline: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst

title: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
description: Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday and clashes erupted with police there and in other German cities after largely peaceful mas
body: Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday and clashes erupted with police there and in other German cities after largely peaceful mass protests over the cost of living.Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who targeted emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.Thousands earlier joined the demonstrations organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police, AFP news agency reported. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website.Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."

schema.headline: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
